source_snapshot.title: fix(upgrade): stop comparing compass versions across two unrelated series
source_snapshot.body:
## The bug

`compass/.version` is written by two producers in two different version series, and recorded no way to tell them apart:

| producer | writes | series |
|---|---|---|
| `release.yml` | the **Ix** version (`0.9.2`) | Ix |
| `install.sh` / `install.ps1` / the compass-upgrade path | the **ix-compass-dist** release (`0.3.0`) | compass |

`isNewer(compassLatest, compassCurrent)` compared whichever happened to be on disk against the dist series. That is correct only while Ix's numbers are the larger ones. **The first ix-compass-dist tag above the running Ix version** — a v1.0.0, or just a v0.9.2 — makes `isNewer` true and replaces a *newer* bundled compass with an older dist build.

Same class as #365/#366, reached from the other end: there the stamp was missing so `current` read as `none`; here the stamp is present but denominated in the wrong series.

## It is not only latent

`install.sh` stamped every install with the latest **dist** release number regardless of where the compass came from. The compass it installs always comes from the release tarball — so it mislabelled a release bundle as a dist build, and clobbered the correct stamp the tarball already carried.

Reproduced on a live v0.9.x install:

```
~/.ix/cli/compass/.version   → 0.2.0     # written by install.sh, from ix-compass-dist
~/.ix/.version-check.json    → compassLatest: 0.3.0
```

`ix` prints "Compass update available" and `ix upgrade` would replace a bundle built from system-compass `main` at v0.9.x release time with dist v0.3.0.

## The fix

The stamp declares its own provenance, and the comparison only runs where it means something:

```
source=release        source=dist
ix=0.9.3              version=0.3.0
compass=7f98724
```

**A release bundle is never replaced by a dist download.** It was built from `main` when the CLI was cut, so it is at least as new as any dist release published before it; one published after arrives with the next Ix release, which bundles `main` again.

The dist download stays the **repair** path for a missing or gutted bundle. That still fires: `getInstalledCompassVersion()` reports `0.0.0` when `index.html` is absent, which no real release number matches.

## Backwards compatibility

A bare number is a legacy stamp — everything shipped up to and including v0.9.2 — and reads as **dist-series**. That is what `install.sh` wrote, it is the majority of installs in the wild, and it leaves them exactly as correct as they are today. Release-bundled legacy stamps stay accidentally-correct until compass-dist passes the Ix version, i.e. no worse than before. New releases carry the explicit form and are immune.

## Why the commit, not a version

`system-compass`'s `package.json` version is not maintained against the dist release series — it reads `0.2.0` while dist is on `v0.3.0` (built from `7f98724`). So stamping the package version would have been a third wrong number. The commit is the only reliable identity the bundle has, and it is passed from the `compass` job to `build` as a job output.

## Both installers stop calling ix-compass-dist

Neither ever installs from there, so neither needs to know what it has published. `resolve_compass_version` / `Get-CompassLatestVersion` are removed. `ix upgrade` asks that question, at the one point where it can also tell which series the installed bundle belongs to.

Each installer now prefers the stamp the tarball shipped with, and only writes one if the bundle has none.

## Tests

`upgrade-compass-stamp.test.ts` — release form, dist form, bare legacy number, empty/malformed, CRLF (how a Windows bundle arrives), and a case pinning the inversion itself.

728 tests green. `bash -n` and `sh -n` clean on install.sh; release.yml parses and `needs.compass.outputs.sha` resolves in the `build` job.

Fixes #376

@@ -59,6 +59,13 @@ jobs:
   compass:
     if: ${{ github.event_name != 'pull_request' }}
     runs-on: ubuntu-latest
+    outputs:
+      # The system-compass commit this bundle was built from. Recorded in the
+      # bundle's .version stamp so a build is identifiable after the fact —
+      # system-compass's package.json version is not maintained against the
+      # ix-compass-dist release series (it read 0.2.0 while dist was on v0.3.0),
+      # so the commit is the only reliable identity the bundle has.
+      sha: ${{ steps.build-compass.outputs.sha }}
     steps:

       - name: Build System Compass
+        id: build-compass

           COMPASS_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.COMPASS_TOKEN }}
         run: |
@@ -98,6 +106,9 @@ jobs:

             }

+          # Capture the source commit before building, so the stamp written in
+          # the package job can identify this bundle (see the job's `outputs`).
+          echo "sha=$(git rev-parse --short HEAD)" >> "$GITHUB_OUTPUT"

+          # back to `unknown`, which is fine because no bundle is staged either.
+          COMPASS_SHA: ${{ needs.compass.outputs.sha }}
         run: |
           STAGING="ix-${VERSION}-${TARGET}"

@@ -282,16 +296,33 @@ jobs:
             # Windows an unrelated tar failure masked it, and everywhere else the
             # swap succeeded and silently reverted the map to a June build.
             #
-            # The Ix version rather than a compass version: the bundle is built
-            # from compass main at release time, so it is always at least as new
-            # as any ix-compass-dist release cut before it. That makes the Ix
-            # version a monotonic stand-in, and isNewer() still offers a genuine
-            # dist upgrade published later at a higher number.
+            # The `+release.<sha>` marker is load-bearing, not decoration. This
+            # bundle is built from system-compass main and has no
+            # ix-compass-dist release number, so the version recorded here is an
+            # *Ix* version. install.sh and the compass-upgrade path write the
+            # same file with a *dist* version. Until v0.9.2 the stamp was a bare
+            # number with no way to tell the two apart, so
+            # `isNewer(distLatest, stamp)` compared two unrelated series and was

+            # the first dist tag above the running Ix version would have

-            # install.sh writes this same file after extracting, using the dist
-            # release number. Either value suppresses the spurious update; the

-            printf '%s' "$VERSION" > "$STAGING/compass/.version"
+            # ONE LINE, and semver build metadata rather than key=value. This
+            # file has readers we cannot upgrade: every already-shipped CLI
+            # reads it with `readFileSync(...).trim()` — the whole file — and

+            printf '%s+release.%s\n' \

@@ -132,10 +132,11 @@ resolve_backend_version() {
     | sed -n 's/.*"tag_name"[[:space:]]*:[[:space:]]*"v\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' || true
 }
 
-resolve_compass_version() {
-  _fetch "https://api.github.com/repos/${GITHUB_ORG}/ix-compass-dist/releases/latest" 2>/dev/null \
-    | sed -n 's/.*"tag_name"[[:space:]]*:[[:space:]]*"v\([^"]*\)".*/\1/p' || true

 # -- Detect platform --
 
@@ -886,6 +887,7 @@ check_installed_version() {
 # specific release, and every build before #259 did publish darwin-amd64 — so a
 # pinned rollback is allowed through to the normal download-and-404 handling.
 SKIP_CLI_INSTALL=0
+CLI_EXTRACTED=0
 if [ "$PLATFORM" = "darwin-amd64" ] && [ -z "${IX_VERSION:-}" ]; then
   echo ""
   warn "Ix does not publish a pre-built CLI for Intel Macs (darwin-amd64)."
@@ -919,6 +921,10 @@ if [ "$SKIP_CLI_INSTALL" = "0" ] && [ -x "$IX_BIN/ix" ]; then
 fi
 
 if [ "$SKIP_CLI_INSTALL" = "0" ] && { [ ! -x "$IX_BIN/ix" ] || [ "$(check_installed_version)" != "$VERSION" ]; }; then
+  # Records that the compass now under $IX_HOME/cli came out of THIS release
+  # tarball. The stamp block near the end of the script needs to know: it must
+  # never label a bundle it did not install (Ix#376).
+  CLI_EXTRACTED=1
   mkdir -p "$INSTALL_DIR"
 
   TMP_DIR=$(mktemp -d)
@@ -1076,9 +1082,38 @@ BACKEND_VER=$(resolve_backend_version)
 # Windows path. Keep the -f test on index.html: stamping a version for a
 # compass that is not on disk is what made `ix upgrade` skip the repair
 # download and break `ix view` permanently.
-COMPASS_VER=$(resolve_compass_version)
-if [ -n "$COMPASS_VER" ] && [ -f "$IX_HOME/cli/compass/index.html" ]; then
-  printf '%s' "$COMPASS_VER" > "$IX_HOME/cli/compass/.version"
+#
+# The compass installed here always comes from the release tarball, never from
+# ix-compass-dist — so it must be stamped as a *release* bundle. This used to
+# write the latest ix-compass-dist release number instead, which mislabelled a
+# release bundle as a dist build and clobbered the correct stamp the tarball
+# already carried. The result was live on real installs: a v0.9.x bundle
+# stamped `0.2.0`, against a dist latest of `0.3.0`, so `ix upgrade` reported an
+# update and would have *downgraded* the bundle to an older build (Ix#376).
+#
+# Prefer the stamp the tarball shipped with, which since v0.9.3 carries the
+# source commit too. Only write one if the bundle has none — tarballs up to
+# v0.9.2 predate the stamp.
+#
+# Gated on CLI_EXTRACTED, and that gate is the whole correctness argument. This
+# block runs even when the CLI install was skipped: the version on disk already
+# matched, or SKIP_CLI_INSTALL=1 on darwin-amd64. In that case the compass under
+# cli/ is whatever was already there, which can be an *ix-compass-dist* bundle
+# left unstamped by an interrupted `ix upgrade` (its stage="stamp" failure
+# installs the bundle and then fails to write .version). Stamping that
+# `+release` would freeze it: shouldOfferCompassUpgradeFor refuses every future
+# dist update for a release bundle, so a genuinely stale compass would never be
+# replaced and `ix upgrade` would print a claim about it that is simply untrue.
+#
+# Nothing is lost by skipping it. When we DID extract, the tarball's own stamp
+# has already landed and is authoritative — which is also what repairs an
+# install mislabelled by the pre-#376 installer. One line, semver build
+# metadata: see the note in release.yml on why this file must stay readable by
+# already-shipped CLIs.
+if [ -f "$IX_HOME/cli/compass/index.html" ]; then
+  if [ "$CLI_EXTRACTED" = "1" ] && [ ! -s "$IX_HOME/cli/compass/.version" ]; then
+    printf '%s+release\n' "$VERSION" > "$IX_HOME/cli/compass/.version"
+  fi
 elif [ ! -f "$IX_HOME/cli/compass/index.html" ]; then
   warn "System Compass is not installed at $IX_HOME/cli/compass — 'ix view' is unavailable until you run 'ix upgrade', which will fetch it."
 fi

commits.message:
fix(upgrade): stop comparing compass versions across two unrelated series

`compass/.version` is written by two producers in two different version series,
and recorded no way to tell them apart:

  - the release workflow stamps the bundle it ships with the **Ix** version
    (`0.9.2`), because that bundle is built from system-compass `main` and has no
    ix-compass-dist release number of its own;
  - install.sh and the compass-upgrade path stamp the **ix-compass-dist** release
    they downloaded (`0.3.0`).

`isNewer(compassLatest, compassCurrent)` compared whichever of those happened to
be on disk against the dist series. That is correct only while Ix's numbers are
the larger ones. The first ix-compass-dist tag above the running Ix version — a
v1.0.0, or just a v0.9.2 — makes `isNewer` true and replaces a *newer* bundled
compass with an older dist build. Same failure as #365/#366, reached from the
other end.

It is not only latent. install.sh stamped every install with the latest *dist*
release number regardless of where the compass came from, mislabelling the
release bundle it had just extracted and clobbering the correct stamp the
tarball carried. A v0.9.x install reads `0.2.0` against a dist latest of
`0.3.0`, so `ix upgrade` reports an update and would downgrade the bundle.

The stamp now declares its own provenance and the comparison only runs where it
means something:

    source=release      source=dist
    ix=0.9.3            version=0.3.0
    compass=7f98724

A release bundle is never replaced by a dist download — it was built from `main`
when the CLI was cut, so it is at least as new as any dist release published
before it, and one published after arrives with the next Ix release, which
bundles `main` again. The dist download stays the *repair* path for a missing or
gutted bundle: that still fires, because `getInstalledCompassVersion()` reports
`0.0.0` when `index.html` is absent, which no real release number matches.

A bare number is a legacy stamp (everything up to v0.9.2) and reads as
dist-series — what install.sh wrote, the majority of installs in the wild, and
no less correct than today. New releases carry the explicit form and are immune.

The commit is recorded because system-compass's package.json version is not
maintained against the dist release series — it read 0.2.0 while dist was on
v0.3.0 — so the commit is the only reliable identity a bundle has.

Both installers stop asking ix-compass-dist what it has published. Neither ever
installs from there; `ix upgrade` asks that question, at the one point where it
can also tell which series the installed bundle belongs to.

Fixes #376

fix(upgrade): make the release-bundle guard reachable from a test

`shouldOfferCompassUpgrade` read the stamp itself, so the only thing the new
tests could reach was `parseCompassStamp`. Deleting the
`source === "release"` branch — the entire behavioural change in #376 — left
all 728 tests green while restoring the inversion in full.

Take the stamp as an argument and export the decision. `installedCompass()`
now returns the whole stamp instead of the version alone, which also stops
the function reading `compass/.version` twice per call.

Tests cover the inversion itself, the dist-series comparison that must still
happen, the repair path for a gutted bundle (which is why the 0.0.0 check
sits ahead of the source check — reversing them is #365/#366 again), the
offline case, and a legacy bare stamp. Both mutations now fail the suite.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

fix(upgrade): keep the compass stamp readable by already-shipped CLIs

The key=value stamp is unreadable by every CLI already in the wild, and the
shipped CLI is exactly what reads it during the upgrade that installs it:
`ix upgrade` swaps in the new tree, then the still-running old process
continues into its own compass block and reads the file it just wrote.

That reader is getTrackedVersion — readFileSync(...).trim(), the whole file —
feeding splitVersion. Measured against origin/main's own isNewer:

  dist 0.3.0 vs "source=release\nix=0.9.4\n..."  -> false  (garbled print)
  dist 0.3.0 vs "source=release\nix=1.0.0\n..."  -> TRUE
  dist 0.3.0 vs "source=release\nix=1.1.0\n..."  -> TRUE

The major parses as NaN -> 0, so at the first 1.x release every older CLI
downloads ix-compass-dist over the newer bundle it just installed — #376
reintroduced by the format change itself.

Provenance now rides in semver build metadata on one line:

  0.9.3+release.7f98724     release bundle
  0.3.0                     dist download (bare, as it has always been)

splitVersion already drops everything after `+`, so old CLIs read 0.9.3 and
behave exactly as they do today.

Also from the same review:

- `present` (index.html on disk) replaces version "0.0.0" as the repair
  trigger. 0.0.0 is also what a stamp truncated by a full disk parses to, and
  repairing on that downgrades an intact release bundle.
- install.sh only stamps when it actually extracted the tarball. The block
  runs even when the install was skipped, where the compass on disk can be an
  unstamped *dist* bundle — labelling that `+release` froze it against every
  future compass update. When we did extract, the tarball's own stamp has
  already landed and repairs a mislabelled install.
- New producer drift test: reads release.yml, install.sh and install.ps1,
  renders each stamp literal and pushes it through the real parser. Three
  producers in three languages with no compile-time link to the reader is how
  this class of bug keeps happening. Verified non-vacuous — restoring the
  multi-line form fails both properties.

744 green. bash -n / sh -n clean, release.yml parses, install.ps1 parses.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

reviews.body:
The diagnosis is right and the live reproduction settles it — `.version` really was denominated in the wrong series, and `source=` is the correct shape for the answer. Checked the parts that could bite:

- `build` does declare `needs: compass`, so `needs.compass.outputs.sha` resolves; on a PR dry-run compass is skipped and the `${COMPASS_SHA:-unknown}` fallback covers it.
- No leftover callers of `resolve_compass_version` / `Get-CompassLatestVersion` — both survive only as comments.
- `$Version` is assigned at `install.ps1:207`, well above the stamp block at :532.
- The `0.0.0` repair check correctly sits *ahead* of the source check, so a gutted release bundle is still repaired rather than pinned forever.

**One gap, fixed in c415461.** `shouldOfferCompassUpgrade` read the stamp itself, so the only thing the new test file could reach was `parseCompassStamp` — a pure function that was never the bug. I deleted the `readCompassStamp().source === "release"` line, which is the entire behavioural change here, and all 728 tests passed. The case named `pins the inversion the marker exists to prevent` survives it too: `expect(parseCompassStamp(...).source).toBe("release")` restates the parser rather than the decision.

Made the decision take the stamp as an argument (`shouldOfferCompassUpgradeFor`) and exported it. `installedCompass()` now returns the whole stamp rather than the version alone, which also drops a second read of `compass/.version` per call.

Five cases now cover it: the inversion, the dist-series comparison that must still happen, the repair path for a gutted bundle, the offline case, and a legacy bare stamp. Two mutations verified failing — deleting the source check, and swapping it ahead of the `0.0.0` check (that one is #365/#366 again: `ix view` never repairs).

733 green.

Retracting my earlier approval. A deeper review turned up a blocking backward-compatibility break that I verified empirically, so this should not merge in its current form.

## Blocking: the new stamp format is unreadable by every already-shipped CLI

The shipped reader is `getTrackedVersion` (`upgrade.ts:199-206`) — `readFileSync(...).trim()`, i.e. **the whole file**. The upgrade sequence matters here: `ix upgrade` swaps in the new tree (including the new-format `compass/.version`), and then the *still-running old process* continues into its own compass block and reads that file with the old parser.

I ran the new format through `origin/main`'s own `isNewer`:

```
dist 0.3.0 vs release-stamp 0.9.4 -> isNewer=false
dist 0.3.0 vs release-stamp 1.0.0 -> isNewer=TRUE
dist 0.3.0 vs release-stamp 1.1.0 -> isNewer=TRUE
dist 0.3.0 vs legacy bare  0.9.4 -> isNewer=false
```

`splitVersion` yields `Number("source=release\nix=1") = NaN -> 0` for the major, so a 1.x release parses as `[0,0,0]`. Today (0.9.x) the damage is a garbled three-line version string in `[ok] Compass already on the latest version (...)`. **At the first 1.0.0 release, every CLI older than this one downloads ix-compass-dist over the newer bundled compass** — the exact #376 downgrade this PR exists to prevent, caused by the format change itself.

Suggested fix that keeps the whole design: make the stamp a **single-line semver with build metadata**, `0.9.4+release.7f98724`. `splitVersion` already does `v.split("+")[0]` with the comment "Build metadata (`+sha`) never participates in precedence" — so old CLIs read `0.9.4` and behave exactly as they do today, while `parseCompassStamp` reads the `+release.<sha>` suffix for provenance. Dist stays a bare number, which is already the legacy-compatible form.

## Also blocking

**`0.0.0` is overloaded** (`upgrade.ts:298`). The doc comment says only a missing `index.html` produces it, but `parseCompassStamp` also returns `{source:"release", version:"0.0.0"}` for a release stamp missing its `ix=` key — a `.version` truncated by a full disk or a kill during the non-atomic write. With the bundle perfectly serviceable, the repair branch fires ahead of the source check and downgrades it. Worth distinguishing "absent" from "malformed" explicitly rather than through the version number.

**`install.sh:1094` stamps `source=release` on a compass it did not install.** The stamp block runs even when the CLI install was skipped (`check_installed_version` == `$VERSION`, or `SKIP_CLI_INSTALL=1`). If `compass/` holds an unstamped *dist* bundle — reachable via `ix upgrade`'s own `stage="stamp"` failure, or Ctrl-C between extract and stamp — it is now permanently labelled `release`, and `shouldOfferCompassUpgradeFor` refuses every future compass update while printing "Compass is the build bundled with Ix <v>", which is false. The deleted code re-stamped with the dist number and stayed self-correcting.

**`install.sh:1093`'s `[ ! -s .version ]` never repairs a mislabelled stamp** — so the fix does not reach the installs the PR body calls the majority in the wild. Re-running the installer on an already-current version skips the extract, so no tarball stamp is laid down, and the bare `0.3.0` survives.

**`IX_VERSION=0.9.0` pins** stamp `source=release ix=0.9.0` onto a months-old bundle and exempt it from dist upgrades forever. `resolve_version` also falls back to `0.1.0` when the API is unreachable.

## Non-blocking

Gating the compass block behind `shouldOfferCompassUpgrade` also gates the orphan sweep inside it. `main` has exactly two sweep sites — one behind "CLI needs updating", one behind "compass needs updating" — and the second exists as the fallback for the first, per its own comment. After this change a user on the latest CLI with a release compass sweeps nothing. I traced it and the severe cases self-heal (a gutted compass reports 0.0.0 and repairs; an interrupted CLI upgrade leaves the CLI stale), so this is stranded orphan directories rather than breakage — but it undercuts #392's reason for sweeping downloads at all.

The diagnosis and the live reproduction in the PR body are right, and the provenance idea is the correct answer. It is the encoding that needs to change.

Addressed in 3f70e75. Re-verified end to end.

**Stamp format.** Provenance now rides in semver build metadata on one line — `0.9.3+release.7f98724` for a release bundle, a bare number for dist. `splitVersion` already drops everything after `+`, so every already-shipped CLI reads `0.9.3` and behaves exactly as it does today. The design intent is unchanged; only the encoding moved.

**`present` replaces the `0.0.0` sentinel.** `installedCompass()` carries whether `index.html` is on disk, so a stamp truncated mid-write no longer masquerades as a missing bundle and triggers a downgrade of an intact one. The present-check still sits ahead of the source-check, so a gutted release bundle is repaired.

**install.sh only stamps what it installed.** Gated on a new `CLI_EXTRACTED` flag. The block runs even when the install was skipped, and in that case the compass on disk can be an unstamped dist bundle — labelling that `+release` froze it against every future update. When we did extract, the tarball's own stamp has already landed, which is also what repairs a mislabelled install. `install.ps1` needs no such gate: it has no already-current skip path.

**New producer drift test.** `upgrade-compass-stamp-producers.test.ts` reads `release.yml`, `install.sh` and `install.ps1`, renders the literal each one writes, and pushes it through the real `parseCompassStamp`. Three producers in three languages with no compile-time link to the reader is how this class of bug keeps recurring. Verified non-vacuous — restoring the multi-line form fails both properties it asserts.

Mutations re-run against the reworked code: deleting the release guard fails two cases, and reverting the stamp producer fails two more.

744 green. `bash -n` and `sh -n` clean on install.sh, release.yml parses, install.ps1 parses clean.

Left as-is deliberately: an `IX_VERSION` pin stamps `+release` on that release's bundle and exempts it from dist upgrades. That reads correct to me — the user pinned a release, and the repair path still fires if the bundle is gutted — but flagging it since the review raised it.
